The Story of Gurudatt Muni

I bow to the five supreme beings — Arhants, Siddhas, Acharyas, Upadhyays, and Sadhus — by whose grace the supreme wealth of omniscience can be attained, and I write the sacred story of Gurudatt Muni.

Gurudatt was the son of the righteous King Vijaydatt and Queen Vijaya of Hastinapur. From childhood, his nature was grave, patient, simple, and courteous. He was unmatched in beauty too. Truly, the glory of merit is boundless.

Vijaydatt handed the kingdom to Gurudatt and himself became a monk, attending to his soul's welfare. Gurudatt took the reins of government and began ruling with great care and moral integrity. The people were very happy. They praised their new king a thousand times over. The people of Gurudatt's kingdom did not even know what suffering meant, for whenever anyone had even the slightest trouble, Gurudatt would immediately come to their aid. He helped everyone with his body, mind, and wealth.

In the land of Lat, near the Droniman Mountain, stood the beautiful city of Chandrapuri. Its king was Chandrakirti, whose queen was Chandralekha. They had a daughter named Abhayamati. Gurudatt proposed to Chandrakirti, asking for Abhayamati's hand in marriage. But Chandrakirti flatly refused — he would not agree to marry Abhayamati to Gurudatt. Gurudatt felt insulted. He became angry with Chandrakirti and immediately launched an attack on Chandrapuri, surrounding it on all sides.

Princess Abhayamati was already captivated by Gurudatt. When she learned that he had besieged Chandrapuri, she went to her father and said, "Father, I do not think it proper to speak about my own affairs, but I must speak so that no obstacle comes to my happiness. For you would not wish to see me in distress even in a dream. My prayer is this: please arrange my marriage with Gurudatt. In that alone lies my happiness."

The generous-hearted Chandrakirti agreed to his daughter's wish. After choosing an auspicious day, he married Abhayamati to Gurudatt with great joy and celebration. Through this alliance, the two kingdoms were united in peace.

Gurudatt and Abhayamati ruled together with justice and compassion. They worshipped Lord Jina daily, gave generously to the worthy, and protected their subjects. In time, they recognised the impermanence of worldly life. They renounced their kingdoms, took initiation as monks, and practised intense austerities. Through dedicated spiritual practice, they destroyed their karmas and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that even anger and pride can become the catalyst for spiritual awakening. Gurudatt's initial insult and attack led to a marriage that ultimately brought both him and his wife to the path of dharma. The wise should understand that all experiences — pleasant or unpleasant — can be used for spiritual growth if one remains mindful of the ultimate goal of liberation.
